To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the uptake of social security benefit increased substantially in long-term survivors of childhood and adolescent cancers, and that the most common causes of social security benefits were diseases of the central nervous system and injury and poisoning.
the uptake of social security benefit among 5-year survivors of childhood, adolescent, and young adult cancer increased substantially.
the uptake of social security benefit was 4.4-fold higher in long-term survivors of childhood, adolescent, and young adult cancer than in the background population.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the health and welfare of cancer survivors in Norway.
long-term medical consequences among cancer survivors and their uptake of social security benefit, which is of importance in the welfare system of the country.
the social security system in Norway and its use among cancer survivors in childhood, adolescence or young adulthood.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the survivors of malignancies of the nervous system and of the haematological system had the highest risks for social security benefits uptake.
the survivors of malignancies in childhood and young adulthood have a higher risk of social welfare benefits uptake than cancer-free peers.

cancer survivors have a high risk of social security benefits, and that this is especially true for survivors of CNS tumours and malignancies of bone, connective tissues and the haematopoetic system, which are all known to have a high prevalence of severe late effects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the uptake of social security benefit is an important outcome measure in cancer survivorship studies.
cancer in childhood, adolescent and young adults is associated with a high risk of long-term medical complications.
the uptake of social security benefit is a valid and useful outcome measure to describe the burden of the long-term consequences of cancer in childhood and young adulthood. © The Author(s) 2019.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the long-term medical consequences among young survivors are severe and may require lifelong care and follow-up.
the risk of social security benefits increases with the severity of cancer, and the risk is highest for survivors of CNS tumours, bone and connective tissue tumours and haematological malignancies.
cancer survivors in Norway have a higher risk of social welfare benefit uptake than the general population.
